full_judgment: 26. In the instant case, the presence of PW 1 on the boat only a few feet away from her husband when he was gunned down, was proved by a number of witnesses such as PWs 2, 3, 4 and 5, all of them, in course of their depositions before the Court, mentioned the presence of PW 1, among others, in the ordinary course of their depositions. True it is that in their earlier statements before the police they did not specifically mention about her presence. But this was a mere omission on their part. Besides, the statements under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the Police during investigation are neither sacrosanct nor even evidence. It is not signed by the maker of the statements and the law never permits such statements before the police to be treated as evidence, because the witnesses may be over enthusiastic and over zealous in making their statements behind the back of the accused. They even may make obliging statements before the police, as such, in the interest of justice and fairplay, those statements, in course of investigation before the police are not treated as evidence. The burden of proof as to whether an accused has committed a crime or not, is always, under section 101 of the Evidence Act, upon the prosecution. The prosecution must, by adducing evidence, prove its allegations before the Court, beyond reasonable doubt. The learned Judge would consider the allegations against an accused only on the basis of evidence led before him. He would consider the testimony of a witness stated in his examination-in-chief, duly tested in his cross-examination and then would weigh the probative value of such evidence produced before him.
